newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan passes law for sweeping forex liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: Japan passes law for sweeping forex liberalisation.

text.p: Japan passed a law on Friday that will bring sweeping reform of foreign exchange rules and take the country a major step towards achieving its "Big Bang" plan for freeing up financial markets.

The reform bill, which was passed by parliament's Upper House, is the first such fundamental review of currency controls in 17 years and is expected to spur new business opportunities and increase competition in the market.

The plan is the centrepiece of the Japanese government's "Big Bang" drive to strip away rules which have stifled domestic markets and left them lagging other financial centres such as London and New York.
Although passed into law on Friday, the changes will not take effect until April 1998.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka has said that the reform is designed to put the Tokyo market in the same league as other key financial centres.
Officials said the reform will also accelerate the pace of a planned easing of controls on tax systems and securities transactions.
The new law will allow open participation in Tokyo's foreign currency markets, scrapping the current rule under which only foreign exchange banks are allowed to conduct foreign exchange transactions.
It will also do away with numerous anachronistic regulations on cross-border transactions and allow corporations and individuals to deal directly with overseas banks and brokers.
Some believe the impact of the deregulation could also be felt beyond the finance industry, leading to wide use of the dollar as an alternative to the yen in Japanese shops.
A Finance Ministry official has predicted there will be coffee shops where customers can pay in dollars and that travellers from around the world may be able to use dollars to shop in Japan.
But analysts say that if controls on foreign exchange transactions are lifted without deregulation in other areas such as taxes, this could prompt an exodus of Japanese capital to overseas markets.
The reform bill will also allow freer cross-border capital transactions and settlements by individuals and corporations with their overseas counterparts.

Strict regulations, which in the past protected Japanese financial institutions from foreign competition, have left Tokyo far behind other money centres in terms of volume of transactions and foreign participatible comparative figures.
Only 77 foreign companies are listed on the stock market in Tokyo compared with 531 in London and 247 in New York.
Japan's financial markets are said to be hollowing out because foreign financial institutions refuse to come here or are leaving Tokyo for other areas with fewer regulations and lower costs.
